newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Goodman's Hearn sees opportunites in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Goodman's Hearn sees opportunites in Asia.

text.p: Australian food companies are in a relatively strong position to access a potential A$16 billion market in Asia, Goodman Fielder Ltd chief executive David Hearn said on Thursday.

Efficient raw materials production, modern technology, experience in developing markets, good management skills and geographic and time-zone proximity were all strengths which Australian companies could exploit, Hearn told a Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) luncheon meeting.
"This strength is supplemented by Australia's variety of climatic zones, the length of production seasons and the ability to supply 'off-season' products to northern hemisphere markets, Hearn said.
He said Asian food demand was expected to increase by US$160 billion from $525 billion in 1990 to $685 billion by 2000.
An extra two billion people were expected to be born in Asia over the next 30 years, and increasing urbanisation would also drive food demand, he added.
Asian food markets were big enough for Australian companies to make a very good return but they had to be smart and competitive, Hearn said.
"It is no good, as Goodman Fielder did in the past, to rush in with a scatter gun approach to Asia food markets," he said.
"We will not be able to compete in all markets and we will be easily picked off by the multi-national food companies and major domestic Asian players," he added.
Australian companies needed to have a country specific policy, put their best people into Asia, and ensure they chose the right partner and distribution network, Hearn said.
Goodman Fielder, Australia's largest food group with annual sales of about A$2.5 billion, has sold some of its Asian operations in recent years.
The company is focusing its Asian strategy on three areas, including an edible oils joint venture in Indonesia and frozen food joint venture in Taiwan.
